methods.name: Full odds
methods.summary: Wild encounters, gifts and soft resets: 1/8192, decided by DVs.
methods.details: In Generation II a Pokémon is Shiny when its Defense, Speed and Special DVs are all 10 and its Attack DV is 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 14 or 15, which is 8 of the 65,536 DV combinations. DVs are generated when a wild Pokémon appears or a gift / stationary Pokémon is created, so random encounters and soft resets both run at 1/8192. A Shiny flashes with stars when it enters battle and shows an icon on its summary screen.
notes: Eggs are not 1/8192 in these games: an Egg copies its Defense DV and most of its Special DV from one parent, so it can only be Shiny when that parent has Defense 10 and Special 2 or 10. Use "Breeding with a Shiny parent" for Egg hunts.
A species with a 7 male : 1 female gender ratio can never be both female and Shiny (females need an Attack DV of 0–1, Shinies need 2 or more). Only Unown I and V can be Shiny.
The red Gyarados at the Lake of Rage is always Shiny.
Pokémon traded from Red / Blue / Yellow keep their DVs, but Generation I tall-grass, cave and Surf encounters can never have Shiny DVs; fishing, gift, stationary and in-game-trade Pokémon can.

methods.name: Breeding with a Shiny parent
methods.summary: Eggs that inherit DVs from a Shiny parent: 1/64.
methods.details: Each Egg takes its Defense DV and the lower three bits of its Special DV from one parent: Ditto if a Ditto is in the Day-Care, otherwise the parent whose gender is opposite to the baby's. When that parent is Shiny the baby already has Defense 10, and it is Shiny if its random Attack DV is one of the 8 valid values (1/2), its random Speed DV is 10 (1/16) and the random top bit of its Special DV gives 10 rather than 2 (1/2): 1/64. Babies of the same gender as a non-Ditto Shiny parent inherit from the other parent and cannot be Shiny, so the odds per Egg depend on the baby species' gender ratio. Pick the pairing that matches your Day-Care pair and count every Egg hatched.

inputs.label: Day-Care pairing
inputs.description: Which parent is Shiny, and the gender ratio of the species that hatches (the mother's species, or the non-Ditto parent's).

options.label: Shiny Ditto + any partner
options.description: Ditto always donates the DVs: 1/64 for every Egg.

options.label: Shiny father, baby species always female
options.description: Every Egg inherits from the father: 1/64.

options.label: Shiny father, baby species 75% female
options.description: Only female babies can be Shiny: 3/256 per Egg.

options.label: Shiny father, baby species 50% female
options.description: Only female babies can be Shiny: 1/128 per Egg.

options.label: Shiny father, baby species 25% female
options.description: Only female babies can be Shiny: 1/256 per Egg.

options.label: Shiny mother, species 25% female
options.description: Only male babies can be Shiny: 3/256 per Egg.

options.label: Shiny mother, species 50% female
options.description: Only male babies can be Shiny: 1/128 per Egg.

options.label: Shiny mother, species 75% female
options.description: Only male babies can be Shiny: 1/256 per Egg.

checkpoints.label: Shiny Ditto: every Egg inherits from the Shiny parent (published 1/64)
Shiny father, 50% female species (1/2 female x 1/64)

notes: The 1/64 figure published on Bulbapedia is for an Egg that inherits from the Shiny parent (offspring of the opposite gender, or any Egg when the Shiny parent is Ditto). The per-Egg odds for the other pairings (1/128, 3/256, 1/256) are derived from the pokecrystal Day-Care code: the baby's gender comes from its own random Attack DV, and only some of the Attack values for the required gender are Shiny values.

Two Shiny Pokémon can never breed with each other: the Day-Care refuses any pair with equal Defense DVs whose Special DVs match in their lower three bits (equal, or 8 apart). The same rule stops a Shiny parent from breeding with offspring that inherited its DVs.
A Shiny Pokémon bred with an ordinary Ditto never gives Shiny Eggs, because Ditto is always the DV donor. The donor does not have to be Shiny itself; it only needs Defense 10 and Special 2 or 10.

A Shiny father cannot produce Shiny babies of a species with a 7 male : 1 female ratio (female babies have an Attack DV of 0–1), and a Shiny mother of an all-female species cannot pass it on at all, because all of her Eggs inherit from the father. Male-only and genderless species only breed with Ditto. Use a Shiny Ditto for all of these.

A Nidoran♀ mother produces Nidoran♀ and Nidoran♂ Eggs equally often, and each inherits like an all-female or all-male species, so use the 50% female options for her: 1/128 per Egg with a Shiny father or with a Shiny Nidoran♀ mother.

A Shiny Ditto can be made with the Generation I / II Transform glitch: a wild Ditto that uses Transform twice in one battle keeps the DVs of the Pokémon it copied before its last Transform, so if it first copies a Shiny you own and then transforms again, it is caught as a Shiny Ditto. For the second Transform the copied moveset has to contain Transform (or Metronome, which can call it), because the transformed Ditto only has your Pokémon's moves.

Each Egg is created in advance: the first one as soon as the second parent is left at the Day-Care, every later one the moment you collect the Egg before it. Saving in front of the Day-Care Man and resetting does not change the Egg he is already holding.

methods.name: Odd Egg (Crystal)
methods.summary: Crystal's Day-Care gift Egg: 14% Shiny internationally, reportedly 50% in Japanese Crystal.
methods.details: In international Pokémon Crystal the Day-Care Man on Route 34 hands over the Odd Egg (you need a free party slot). At that moment the game picks one of 14 preset Eggs: seven baby species, each in a normal and a Shiny version. Save before talking to him, take the Egg, hatch it (20 Egg cycles) and reset to the save if it is not what you want; each reset is one attempt.

inputs.label: Release / target
inputs.description: Which release you play and whether any Shiny or one particular Shiny species counts as a success.

options.label: Japanese: any Shiny (50%, reported)
options.description: Mobile System GB event Egg; no longer obtainable.

notes: Hatch table from the pokecrystal disassembly, matching Bulbapedia (normal % + Shiny %): Pichu 8 + 1, Cleffa 16 + 3, Igglybuff 16 + 3, Smoochum 14 + 2, Magby 10 + 2, Elekid 12 + 2, Tyrogue 10 + 1, totalling 14% Shiny. Some guides list Tyrogue at 2% Shiny (15% in total); the game data says 1%.
The percentages are stored as rounded 16-bit thresholds, so the exact international rate is 9177/65536 (14.003%).

The contents are fixed when the Egg is handed over, so resetting after you have received it changes nothing. Every Shiny Odd Egg Pokémon has DVs 2 / 10 / 10 / 10 (Attack / Defense / Speed / Special) and every normal one has all zeroes, which also makes every hatchling female except Tyrogue.

The 50% rate for Japanese Crystal is the figure given by both Bulbapedia (citing an archived fan site) and Serebii; it was not checked against Japanese game data here and its per-species split is not documented. In that release the Odd Egg had to be redeemed with an Egg Ticket over the Mobile System GB service, which has shut down, and the Japanese Virtual Console release cannot obtain it.

methods.name: Full odds
methods.summary: Wild encounters, soft resets and Eggs: 1/8192. No boosting methods exist.
methods.details: From Generation III on, a Pokémon is Shiny when Trainer ID xor Secret ID xor the upper and lower halves of its personality value is less than 8, a flat 8 in 65,536. These games have no way to raise that chance, so every wild, stationary, gift and Egg Pokémon is 1/8192: count random encounters, soft resets or hatched Eggs.
notes: Emerald never seeds its random number generator at boot, so every power-on and soft reset starts from seed 0 and advances about 60 times per second. Resets that reach the encounter with the same timing land on the same frame and give the same Pokémon, so vary how long you wait before each encounter.
Ruby and Sapphire seed the generator from the real-time clock at boot. With a dead internal battery the seed is always 0x5A0, which causes the same repeated-frame problem as Emerald.
Shininess depends on your Trainer ID and Secret ID, so a Shiny frame found on someone else's save file will not be Shiny on yours.

methods.name: Full odds
methods.summary: Wild encounters, soft resets and Eggs: 1/8192. No boosting methods exist.
methods.details: From Generation III on, a Pokémon is Shiny when Trainer ID xor Secret ID xor the upper and lower halves of its personality value is less than 8, a flat 8 in 65,536. These games have no way to raise that chance, so every wild, stationary, gift and Egg Pokémon is 1/8192: count random encounters, soft resets or hatched Eggs.
notes: FireRed and LeafGreen start a hardware timer on the title screen and seed the random number generator from it when you continue, so each soft reset normally begins from a different seed (unlike Emerald, which always starts from seed 0).

Unown's Shiny chance varies by form, because the form is also derived from the personality value: 1/5120, 1/6144, 1/9216, 1/10240 or 1/18432 depending on the form and on your Trainer ID and Secret ID.

methods.name: Full odds
methods.summary: Wild encounters, soft resets and same-language Eggs: 1/8192.
methods.details: Every wild, stationary, gift and Egg Pokémon gets a single personality value, and it is Shiny when Trainer ID xor Secret ID xor the two halves of that value is less than 8 (8 in 65,536). Count random encounters, soft resets or hatched Eggs.
notes: Do not lead with a Cute Charm Pokémon while hunting wild Pokémon: when the Ability forces the target's gender, the personality value comes from a tiny fixed set that contains no Shiny value for most Trainer ID / Secret ID combinations. Bulbapedia lists the resulting odds as 1/24576 (a few ID combinations instead reach up to 21.34%).

The Manaphy Egg from Pokémon Ranger is re-rolled when it hatches so that it is never Shiny for the Trainer ID stored in the Egg; it can only turn out Shiny if the Egg is traded to another save file before hatching.
Pokémon in ordinary (non-flashing) Poké Radar patches still have this same 1/8192 chance.

methods.name: Masuda Method
methods.summary: Eggs from parents of different languages: 5 rolls (1/1638.80).
methods.details: Leave two Pokémon with different languages of origin at the Day Care, for example one traded from a foreign-language game. When the Egg is made the game checks its personality value and, if that is not Shiny, re-rolls it up to 4 more times, 5 tries in total. Count each Egg hatched.
notes: What matters is each parent's language of origin, not the language of your save file. Foreign-language in-game trade Pokémon count, such as the Meister's Magikarp (Foppa).
In Generation IV only, an Everstone will not pass down a Nature while the Masuda Method is active.

The Egg's personality value is stored as soon as the Day-Care Man has an Egg, and the Masuda re-rolls are derived from that stored value. Saving once the Egg is ready and soft resetting never changes whether it is Shiny; only its IVs are rolled again when you collect it.
Often quoted as 5/8192 (about 1/1638); the exact chance of at least one hit in 5 tries is 1/1638.8.
The 4 re-rolls are confirmed in the Platinum decompilation and in PokeFinder. Diamond and Pearl share the same parent-language check, but their Egg routine has not been decompiled yet.

methods.name: Poké Radar chaining
methods.summary: Chain one species with the Poké Radar: up to about 1/200 per patch at a chain of 40.
methods.details: Professor Rowan gives you the Poké Radar in Sandgem Town once you have the National Pokédex. Use it in tall grass and enter a shaking patch; knocking out or catching that Pokémon starts a chain, and every further patch that holds the same species adds 1. Each patch that would continue the chain rolls for a forced Shiny, with odds that grow with the chain length and peak at 328/65536 (41/8192, about 1/200) at 40; a Shiny patch flashes white twice. From 40 on, stop entering patches: walk 50 steps to recharge, use the Radar again and repeat until a Shiny patch appears.

inputs.label: Chain length
inputs.description: Consecutive Pokémon of the same species defeated or caught, as shown by the Pokétch chain counter (it stops at 999). The odds stop improving at 40.

checkpoints.label: Chain 0: first Radar use, no forced Shiny (natural 8/65536)
Chain 33 (41/65536): first chain better than the Masuda Method

notes: Odds per patch = (floor(65535 / (8200 - 200 x chain)) + 1) / 65536, with the divisor never going below 200. This is the Platinum decompilation's CheckPatchShiny routine and it reproduces the per-patch table on Bulbapedia's Poké Radar page exactly. The summary table on Bulbapedia's Shiny Pokémon page lists the cap as "41 rolls (~1/200.29)", but the game makes a single 328/65536 check, which is 1/199.80.
At chain 0 (the first Radar use) no patch can be forced Shiny, so only the natural 1/8192 applies. Ordinary patches later in a chain keep that natural chance on top of the table value.

These odds are per patch that is set to continue the chain. Each of the up to four patches first rolls to hold the chained species: 88% / 68% / 48% / 28% for the ring 4 / 3 / 2 / 1 tiles away from you (10 points higher on the patches generated right after a catch), and only patches that pass are checked for a Shiny. With all four patches in grass, a Radar reset at chain 40 shows a Shiny patch about 1.16% of the time (roughly 1/86); the patches that appear right after a catch reach about 1.35% (roughly 1/74). Bulbapedia's Poké Radar page gives the same two percentages; the "four patches, about 1/50" figure on its Shiny Pokémon page leaves out the continue roll.

The chain breaks if you meet a different species, flee or fail to defeat or catch the Pokémon, get into any non-Radar wild battle, ride the Bicycle, let every shaking patch scroll off-screen, or use the Radar and no patch lands in grass. Radar patches ignore Repels, so keep one active. Patches that are set to continue the chain always shake the same way as the patch you entered last, so a patch that shakes differently is never a guaranteed one: it holds an ordinary random encounter and only continues the chain if that happens to be the chained species. Half of the non-guaranteed patches shake the matching way too, so a matching shake is not a guarantee either.
Verified against the Platinum decompilation. Bulbapedia documents Diamond and Pearl with the same routine, but their code has not been decompiled and was not checked directly.

Count random encounters, soft resets or hatched Eggs. The Poké Radar cannot be obtained in these games, so the Masuda Method is the only way to raise the odds.
notes: Chikorita, Cyndaquil and Totodile are all generated and drawn in their real colours on the selection screen, so a starter reset checks three Pokémon at once; see the Starter reset method.
Pokéwalker Pokémon and the Spiky-eared Pichu cannot be Shiny. The red Gyarados at the Lake of Rage always is.

Do not lead with a Cute Charm Pokémon while hunting wild Pokémon: when the Ability forces the target's gender, the personality value comes from a tiny fixed set that contains no Shiny value for most Trainer ID / Secret ID combinations. Bulbapedia lists the resulting odds as 1/24576 (a few ID combinations instead reach up to 21.34%).

methods.name: Starter reset (all three shown)
methods.summary: All three starters are generated and shown before you pick: 3 Pokémon per reset at 1/8192 each.
methods.details: When the starter selection screen in Professor Elm's lab opens, the game creates Chikorita, Cyndaquil and Totodile, each with its own random personality value, and draws each one in its Shiny colours if it is Shiny. Save before opening the selection, look at all three, and soft reset if none is Shiny. Each reset counts as three Pokémon, so the chance that at least one of the three is Shiny is about 1/2731 per reset.

checkpoints.label: Per starter: one personality value each, three starters per reset (8/65536)

notes: If only one particular starter will do, each reset is a single 1/8192 chance for it: use Full odds and count one per reset instead.
A Shiny starter you leave behind is lost: if the rival ends up with it, his copy appears in its normal colours.
This only works in HeartGold and SoulSilver. In most other games the starters are shown in their normal colours until one has been chosen.

methods.summary: Wild encounters, soft resets and same-language Eggs: 1/8192.
methods.details: Every wild, stationary, gift and Egg Pokémon gets a single personality value, and it is Shiny when Trainer ID xor Secret ID xor the two halves of that value is less than 8 (8 in 65,536). Pokémon obtained through the Pokémon Dream World cannot be Shiny.

methods.name: Masuda Method
methods.summary: Eggs from parents of different languages: 6 rolls (1/1365.75).
methods.details: Leave two Pokémon with different languages of origin at the Day Care, for example one traded from a foreign-language game. Generation V raised the bonus to 5 re-rolls, so each Egg gets up to 6 personality values. Count each Egg hatched.
notes: What matters is each parent's language of origin, not the language of your save file; foreign-language in-game trade Pokémon count too.
From Generation V on, an Everstone passes down a Nature normally while the Masuda Method is active.
Often quoted as 6/8192 (about 1/1365); the exact chance of at least one hit in 6 tries is 1/1365.75.

methods.name: Full odds
methods.summary: Wild encounters, soft resets and Eggs: 1/8192, or about 1/2731 with the Shiny Charm.
methods.details: Every wild, stationary and Egg Pokémon gets one personality value at 8 in 65,536. The Shiny Charm, introduced in these games, adds two more tries for 3 in total. Professor Juniper hands it over once you own every Pokémon in the National Pokédex (Mythical Pokémon excluded) and Cedric Juniper has evaluated it. Count random encounters, soft resets or hatched Eggs.
notes: The Shiny Charm works on wild Pokémon, stationary encounters such as Legendary Pokémon, and Eggs. It does nothing for gift Pokémon, in-game trades or Mystery Gifts, so resetting for a gift stays at 1/8192.

Shiny-locked in Black 2 and White 2: Reshiram, Zekrom, every Hidden Grotto Pokémon, the gift Eevee from Castelia City and the gift Deerling on Route 6. Dream Radar and Dream World Pokémon cannot be Shiny either.
Guaranteed Shinies: the Haxorus in the Nature Preserve (after registering every non-event Pokémon in the Unova Pokédex) and Benga's gift Gible (Black 2) or Dratini (White 2).
Lucky Power at its third level adds one more roll to wild and stationary encounters; see the Lucky Power method.

methods.name: Masuda Method
methods.summary: Eggs from parents of different languages: 6 rolls (1/1365.75), 8 with the Shiny Charm (1/1024.44).
methods.details: Leave two Pokémon with different languages of origin at the Day Care, for example one traded from a foreign-language game. Each Egg gets up to 6 personality values, and the Shiny Charm adds its two tries on top for 8. Count each Egg hatched.

checkpoints.label: Masuda Method + Shiny Charm, 8 personality values (published 8/8192)

notes: What matters is each parent's language of origin, not the language of your save file; foreign-language in-game trade Pokémon count too.
From Generation V on, an Everstone passes down a Nature normally while the Masuda Method is active.
Often quoted as 6/8192 and 8/8192 (about 1/1365 and 1/1024); the exact figures are 1/1365.75 and 1/1024.44.

methods.name: Lucky Power ↑↑↑ (Pass Power)
methods.summary: Entralink Pass Power that adds one Shiny roll to wild and stationary encounters.
methods.details: Lucky Power is a Pass Power added in Black 2 and White 2. While its third level (↑↑↑: 30 Pass Orbs, unlocked at Black and White Entree levels of 49, lasts 3 minutes) is active, wild and stationary Pokémon get one extra personality value on top of the base roll and the Shiny Charm's two. Activate it, hunt with random encounters or soft resets as usual, and re-activate it whenever it runs out.

checkpoints.label: Lucky Power ↑↑↑ + Shiny Charm, 4 personality values

notes: Lucky Power ↑ and ↑↑ only change which species appear and add no roll. Bulbapedia's Pass Power table also lists the roll for the 10-minute Lucky Power S (50 Pass Orbs); PokeFinder only models the ↑↑↑ level. Serebii calls this Pass Power "Charm Power" and lists the same costs, Entree levels and durations.
It does not affect Eggs, gift Pokémon or Shiny-locked encounters, and it does not exist in Black and White.

This is a comparatively recent finding: it is implemented in PokeFinder's Generation V wild and stationary generators and listed in Bulbapedia's Pass Power table, but Bulbapedia's main Shiny-rate table does not include it. The odds shown here are computed from the roll count rather than quoted from a published table.

methods.name: Full odds
methods.summary: Wild encounters and soft resets: 1/4096, or 3 rolls (1/1365.67) with the Shiny Charm.
methods.details: Every wild or stationary Pokémon gets one Shiny roll at 1/4096, the rate introduced in Generation VI. With the Shiny Charm the game generates up to two extra personality values, for three rolls in total. Count one encounter per wild Pokémon seen or per soft reset.
notes: The Shiny Charm does not affect gift Pokémon or Mystery Gift Pokémon; those keep a single roll. In-game trades cannot be Shiny at all. Stationary encounters that are not Shiny-locked do get the charm rolls.
Shiny-locked in X and Y: Articuno, Zapdos, Moltres, Xerneas, Yveltal, Zygarde, Mewtwo and the Snorlax on Route 7, plus the gift Lucario from the Tower of Mastery and all in-game trades.
Eggs use different charm maths (2 rolls with the charm alone, not 3). Use the Breeding or Masuda Method entries for hatching.

methods.name: Breeding (same language)
methods.summary: Eggs from same-language parents: 1/4096, or only 2 rolls (1/2048.25) with the Shiny Charm.
methods.details: Breed two compatible Pokémon that share a language of origin at the Pokémon Day Care on Route 7 and hatch the Eggs. Without the Shiny Charm an Egg gets a single Shiny roll. With the charm the Egg's personality value is rolled twice, not three times, so the charm is worth one net roll here instead of the usual two. Count each hatched Egg as one encounter.

checkpoints.label: Egg with Shiny Charm only (2 rolls)

notes: 8191/16777216 is the exact value of 1 - (4095/4096)^2, i.e. two rolls. It is written as a fixed case because the Shiny Charm is worth one net roll for Eggs.

Sources disagree. Bulbapedia's Shiny Charm page describes the Generation VI-VII charm as two extra rerolls on top of the base roll and says that before Generation VIII the initial roll and both rerolls all count when breeding (3 rolls, about 1/1365.67). 3DSRNGTool's Generation VI Egg generator, which reproduces the game's RNG calls, uses 2 personality-value rolls with the charm, 6 with the Masuda Method and 8 with both, with no separate base roll (an Egg with neither bonus gets its single personality value from the main RNG when it is accepted) — the same structure SciresM documented as an off-by-one for Sword and Shield — and RotomLabs lists Eggs with the charm at 1/2048.25. The tool-derived 2 rolls are used here.
Switching one parent for a Pokémon with a different language of origin turns this into the Masuda Method (6 rolls, 8 with the charm).

methods.name: Masuda Method
methods.summary: Eggs from parents of different languages: 6 rolls (1/683.08), 8 with the Shiny Charm (1/512.44).
methods.details: Leave two compatible Pokémon with different languages of origin at the Pokémon Day Care on Route 7 (a foreign-language Ditto is the usual choice) and hatch the Eggs they produce. Every Egg from such a pair gets extra personality-value rolls: 6 in total, or 8 with the Shiny Charm. Count each hatched Egg as one encounter.
notes: What matters is each parent's language of origin (shown as a language tag on the summary screen from Generation VI), not the language your game is set to. Two parents with the same language of origin get no bonus.

Bulbapedia describes this as 1 base roll + 5 Masuda rerolls (+2 with the Shiny Charm); 3DSRNGTool's Egg generator models it as 6 Masuda rolls (+2 charm) with no base roll. Both give 6 rolls, and 8 with the charm, which is what this entry computes.
Serebii prints the Generation VI rate as '1 in 682.7' (a straight 6/4096); the exact value for 6 independent rolls is 1/683.08.

methods.name: Poké Radar chaining
methods.summary: Chain one species with the Poké Radar: up to 1/100 per chain patch at a chain of 40.
methods.details: Use the Poké Radar in tall grass or flowers, enter a shaking patch, and catch or knock out the Pokémon to start a chain; then keep entering patches that hold the same species. Each chain-continuing (violently shaking) patch is forced Shiny with a chance of 1/8100 at first, and the denominator drops by 200 with every link until it reaches 1/100 at a chain of 40. A Shiny patch visibly sparkles and plays the Shiny sound, so once you reach 40 stop battling and keep re-using the Radar (it has to be recharged by walking) until a sparkling patch appears. Patches in the outer rings are the safest ones to enter.

inputs.label: Chain length
inputs.description: Pokémon of the chained species caught or knocked out in a row (the game stops counting at 9,999). The Shiny patch odds stop improving at 40. After catching a Shiny from a sparkling patch, set this back to 0: the patch rate restarts at 1/8100.

checkpoints.label: Shiny Charm has no effect at chain 40

notes: These odds are per chain-continuing patch, not per Radar use. Each use creates up to four patches (one per ring) that are chain patches 23/43/63/83% of the time from the innermost to the outermost ring (33/53/73/93% if the last Pokémon was caught rather than knocked out), so at a chain of 40+ one Radar use has roughly a 2.1% chance (2.5% after a catch) of showing a sparkling patch (Bulbapedia).

The Shiny Charm does not affect chain patches: a true chain patch is either forced Shiny or forced non-Shiny. Only the regular shaking patches, which hold a random species and can break the chain, use the standard rate including the charm.

With no chain yet (chain 0, the first Radar use) a sparkling patch cannot appear: the decompiled routine forces every chain-type patch non-Shiny while the chain length is 0, and ordinary shaking patches just use the normal wild rate. The 1/8100 entry at 0 is the starting value of the game's separate patch-rate counter (also what Bulbapedia's table prints for 0); it is only live right after that counter has been reset by catching a Shiny.

Catching a Shiny from a sparkling patch resets the patch rate to 1/8100 without ending the chain (the chain-length IV bonus continues), and the rate then improves by 200 per link again, so from that point enter the links made since that catch rather than the full chain. Knocking the Shiny out or re-using the Radar instead does not reset it.

Bonus music: each time the chain continues there is a 2% chance (4% on the player's birthday as set in the 3DS profile) that the music switches to the upbeat 'Poké Radar Chain!' theme. While it plays, chain patches use 1/100 whatever the chain length, and a Shiny caught then does not reset the rate; every Radar use or encounter has a 50% chance to end it.

Patch appearance can lie: a chain patch looks like a regular shaking patch 20% of the time, and a regular patch looks like a violently shaking one 10% of the time, so a violent-looking patch can still break the chain.

The chain ends if you run from a battle, meet a different species, step into the weakly shaking (empty) patch, enter a Horde Encounter or Trainer battle, use Sweet Scent, Honey, a field move, the Dowsing Machine or a fishing rod, pick up an item, ride the Bicycle or Roller Skates (moving with the Circle Pad counts), leave the area, walk until every shaking patch is off-screen, trigger a story event, hatch an Egg, or close the game.
The Radar cannot be used in long grass or in the Friend Safari. A random encounter with the chained species in ordinary grass can continue the chain.

Serebii's Shiny page still prints the Diamond/Pearl/Platinum formula for X and Y as well; the decompiled X/Y routine (wwwwwwzx, Lusamine) uses the 8100 - 200 x chain rate with the 1/100 cap shown here.

methods.name: Chain fishing
methods.summary: Hook Pokémon back to back: +2 rolls per hook, up to 41 rolls (1/100.39) at a chain of 20.
methods.details: Stand still at a fishing spot and keep fishing; every Pokémon you reel in adds one to the chain, whether you catch it, knock it out or run. Each link adds two Shiny rolls, up to a chain of 20 (41 rolls, or 43 with the Shiny Charm), after which the odds stay at the cap. model.spec:
Inputs: searchLevel (integer 0..999, the species' Search Level = times seen), chain (integer >= 0, hidden Pokémon caught or defeated in a row BEFORE this encounter), shinyCharm (boolean).
Output: p = probability that the hidden Pokémon about to be generated is Shiny.

1. Chain position: c = chain mod 100.   // the game's chain counter cycles every 100 encounters; this encounter is number c + 1 of the cycle
2. Target value (integer):
     if searchLevel > 200:      t = searchLevel + 600
     else if searchLevel > 100: t = 2 * searchLevel + 400
     else:                      t = 6 * searchLevel
3. One forced-Shiny check succeeds when a uniform random integer in 0..9999 is < t * 0.01, so
     pCheck = ceil(t / 100) / 10000      // e.g. searchLevel 100 -> 6/10000, 200 -> 8/10000, 201 -> 9/10000, 999 -> 16/10000, 0 -> 0
4. Number of checks before the boost:
     n = 1
     if shinyCharm: n = n + 2
     if c == 49:      n = n + 5          // 50th encounter of the cycle
     else if c == 99: n = n + 10         // 100th encounter of the cycle
5. Boost (+4 checks): guaranteed when c > 0 and (c + 1) mod 5 == 0 (every 5th encounter: c = 4, 9, 14, ..., 99); otherwise it is applied with probability 0.04.
     forced(k) = 1 - (1 - pCheck)^k      // checks are independent; any success forces the Pokémon Shiny
     if c > 0 and (c + 1) mod 5 == 0: pForced = forced(n + 4)
     else:                            pForced = 0.04 * forced(n + 4) + 0.96 * forced(n)
6. If no check succeeds the Pokémon is generated like any wild Pokémon:
     r = 3 if shinyCharm else 1
     pNatural = 1 - (4095 / 4096)^r
7. p = pForced + (1 - pForced) * pNatural

Maximum number of checks is 17 (Shiny Charm, 100th encounter: 1 + 2 + 10 + 4). Report odds as 1 in (1 / p).

Shiny Charm, Search Level 0 (3 natural rolls only)

Bulbapedia states that soft resetting inside the Ultra Space Wilds never changes the outcome, and 3DSRNGTool treats every non-legendary Ultra Space Wilds encounter as Shiny-locked unless the arrival roll forced it Shiny.
